@graph.alternativeHeadline: The repeatable launch-day PR method behind RARI Chain's 11-placement mainnet
@graph.description: A step-by-step teardown of how a coordinated tier-1 launch produced 11 simultaneous placements in a 24-hour news cycle: sell a category not an announcement, give one outlet a real exclusive, pre-build and pre-brief the rest, and hold a hard launch moment. Worked example: the RARI Chain mainnet.

mainEntity.name: Can a founder run this play without a PR agency?

acceptedAnswer.text: Partly. A founder can define the category angle and lock the launch date themselves. The hard, time-boxed parts, negotiating the anchor exclusive, pre-briefing ten desks under separate embargoes, and building publish-ready kits, are where an operator earns the fee, because they hinge on existing reporter relationships and nine days of tight coordination that a founder rarely has bandwidth for during a launch.

mainEntity.name: How far before launch should the biggest placement run?

acceptedAnswer.text: The anchor exclusive publishes at the launch moment, but the reporting runway starts seven to ten days earlier. The RARI mainnet used a nine-day embargo. Some launches deliberately place a major feature a few days ahead of a token event so it is not lost in launch-day noise; for a product or mainnet launch, timing the anchor to the launch minute concentrates the cycle.

mainEntity.name: Does this only work for crypto launches?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The mechanics, one category angle, one anchor exclusive, ten pre-briefed desks, one hard launch moment, are media-agnostic. The worked example is a Web3 mainnet, but the same structure runs for an AI startup product launch or a cybersecurity vendor announcement. What changes is the outlet map and the category argument, not the method.

mainEntity.name: Why an exclusive instead of pitching everyone at once?

acceptedAnswer.text: An exclusive is the only lever that turns a rewrite into a feature. Reporters invest days only when they have something competitors do not. That feature then sets the canonical narrative the rest of the stack lifts from, which is why the sequencing, one exclusive first, then the pre-briefed stack, produces coordinated coverage that a simultaneous blast never does.

mainEntity.name: What is the single biggest reason these launches fail?

acceptedAnswer.text: Positioning. If the story is an announcement rather than a side in an argument the press is already having, no amount of coordination saves it, because there is nothing for the other ten desks to re-report. Every failed launch stack traces back to a category that was never really there.
